At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members to  the meeting of the Committee 
and the representatives of the Ministry of Ports, S hipping and Waterways (M/o PS&W), 
apprising them of the agenda of the meeting i.e. to  deliberate on ‘Progress made in 
implementation of Sagarmala Project.’ 
2.         Initiating the discussion, the Chairman stated that ‘Sagarmala Project’ concept was 
initially approved by the Union Cabinet in 2015 as a part of the National Perspective Plan (NPP), 
which was released by the Hon’ble Prime Minister, f or the development of India’s 7,500 km 
coastline, 14,500 km potentially navigable waterway s and maritime sector. ‘Sagarmala Project’ 
intends to enhance the capacity of major and non-ma jor ports, modernize them, strengthen port 
connectivity and evacuation infrastructure, simplif y procedures adopted in ports, promote usage 
of electronic channels for information exchange lea ding to hassle-free and seamless cargo 
movement. He asked the Secretary to apprise the Com mittee of the efforts made by the Ministry 
towards achieving port-led direct and indirect deve lopment, provision of cost-effective and 
efficient infrastructure in ports, holistic develop ment in harnessing the potential of India's 
coastline and river network and improving export co mpetitiveness. He queried about the 
challenges faced by the ports across the country in  terms of last-mile connectivity, multi-modal 
transportation, connectivity with airways, highways  and railways as envisaged in the ambitious 
Prime Minister's Gati-Shakti National Master Plan a nd measures taken thereof for their 
successful implementation. 
  
3.               It was pointed out by the Chairman  that the infrastructure plan of a country must 
seamlessly & efficiently move goods & people across  various modes of transport. However, this 
requires a coordinated approach, as roads would fee d into railway lines, which in turn would 
feed into ports, efficiently moving goods from the hinterlands to the ports. This would further 
48

 
lead to and enable the development of multiple urba n, industrial centres across India. These 
urban centres in turn, would enable balanced region al development, as multiple industrial 
clusters could sprout up across India. Both Central  as well as various state government revenues 
would be scaled up many times, enabling higher spen ding on social sectors and would have the 
spill-over effect of easing pressure on existing ur ban agglomerations, leading to a higher quality 
of life across the board. 
4.               Furthermore, while many economic z ones, industrial parks, logistics hubs and ports 
have been planned, they often fail to deliver to th eir optimal levels, owing to inefficient multi-
modal connectivity, and also due to their small siz e. The fragmented nature of decision making, 
with each department working in silos meant that a disjointed industrial network was created. 
While several issues have been sorted out, in many areas, some co-ordination issues still remain 
to be resolved and remain unconnected as well. Such  issues are responsible for the lack of scale 
in Indian manufacturing sector which coupled with r elatively inefficient logistics network has 
hampered India's global competitiveness disallowing  us to harness our complete growth 
potential. 
5.               He desired to be apprised of prepa redness of the Ministry in terms of provision of 
sustainable infrastructure to ancillary manufacturi ng clusters in port vicinity, seamless last-mile 
connectivity of ports through multi-modal transport ation, shifting movement of industrial goods 
to coastal and inland waterways, employing funding solutions for NPP and ‘Sagarmala Projects’ 
on Central, State and port level and the obstacles faced by the Ministry. 
6.         The Secretary, M/o PS&W, before making h is presentation, apprised the Committee that 
the Ministry has been working towards modernization  of ports lagging behind in terms of 
connectivity through PPP, technological development  of cargo-handling, multi-modal 
transportation to connect all ports under the PM's ‘Gati-Shakti’ programme, building energy-
49

 
efficient technology to curb waterways pollution, r egulation and operation of ports under the 
Major Port Authorities Act, 2021, planning and impr oving investment in initiatives identified 
under the Vision-2030 policy. The Committee was fur ther apprised of the Ministry’s efforts to 
achieve desired goals in  port-improvement, cargo c ost reduction, smooth and licensed cargo 
handling, maritime safety, developing coastal jetti es and fishing harbours for welfare of the 
fishermen, RORO Pax ferries for seamless transfer o f vehicles, cargo and passengers. He also 
informed the Committee of the enactment of the Majo r Port Authorities Act, 2021, the Marine 
Aids to Navigation Act, 2021 and the New Inland Vessels Act, 2021to boost the port sector. 
7.         Through his presentation the Secretary, M/oPS&W focused on the progress made in the 
‘Sagarmala Projects,’ expanding areas such as Inlan d Waterways cargo volume-growth over the 
last 5 years, coastal traffic growth of 10.2% in Indian Maritime Sector, reduction of logistic costs 
for EXIM and domestic trade, multi-modal transporta tion, monitoring of industries/ 
manufacturing centers vis-a-vis  ports, bridging skill-gap through job creation in the Indian 
maritime sector, port-led industrialization, coasta l community development, jetty/ RORO Pax 
construction in coastal and inland waterways, promo ting coastal and cruise tourism  etc. The 
Committee was apprised of the Institutional Mechani sms employed by the Ministry in 
implementation of the ‘Sagarmala Projects’ viz. Sagarmala Coordination and Steering 
Committee (SCSC) to enable coordination among vario us organizations of the government, 
National Sagarmala Apex Committee (NSAC) to guide a nd review the progress of the project, 
and State Sagarmala Committee (SSC) to oversee Stat e-level coordination over the project. The 
Committee was further apprised of the milestones ac hieved by the Ministry in completion of 181 
projects under the NPP and that the ‘Sagarmala Proj ects’ have borne fruits in the domains of last 
mile rail and road connectivity enhancement, coasta l berths fishing harbor, jetty/ Roll-on-Roll-
off (RORO) ferry construction at Major ports, holis tic development of islands/ coastal districts, 
50

 
etc. The Secretary apprised the Committee that the Ministry is pushing to ensure feasible 
implementation of projects through PPP mode and fun ding of high social impact projects with 
zero Internal Rate of Return (IRR) through Sagarmala Programme. 
8.         The Committee was also informed of the e stablishment of Technological centers/ 
institutes for Maritime and Shipbuilding research a nd training, skill development 
training,  functioning under the ‘Sagarmala Project s’ Scheme, viz. Center of Excellence in 
Maritime and Shipbuilding (CEMS), National Technolo gy Center for Ports, Waterways and 
Coasts (NTCPWC), and Center for Inland and Coastal Maritime Technology (CICMT) with the 
intent to make India a leading player in shipbuildi ng, innovative ship-designing, cryogenic cargo 
handling and renewable energy harvesting from inland waters. 
9.         The Chairman, while mentioning about the  recent Study Visit of the Committee to 
Andaman and Nicobar Islands, expressed his disappoi ntment at the lack of coordination among 
various Ministries/ Departments/ Agencies and the n eed for a master-plan thereof to tackle 
transportation issues arising in interlinking ports  with railways, airways and roadways. He also 
stated that marketing is crucial to identify and de velop tourism at Andaman and Nicobar Islands. 
He also suggested that Ministry should assign matte rs relating to safety/ security at ports, as per 
ISO Standards, to affordable private agencies. He p ointed out that as tourism is also an aspect of 
Sagarmala Project, in addition to goods transfer he  suggested that the Ministry should ensure 
connectivity facilities to attract tourists, such a s building tourist terminals and hotels. He also 
mentioned about a specific Maritime University, und er the Ministry, where funds have been 
unscrupulously withdrawn, from the development fund s/ Grants of Autonomous bodies/ 
Universities and desired that recoveries should be initiated and strict action should be taken 
against them. He expressed the dire need to have tr ained staff to manage shortage in Civil 
51

 
Aviation, Tourism and Shipping sectors and expediti ous system to obtaining environmental 
clearance from Ministry of Environment for future port projects. 
10.         Members raised several queries such as ferry development of ferries, public amenities 
around areas connecting all three sectors viz. tourism, aviation and ports, development of 
lighthouses and coastlines. The Chairman then direc ted that written replies to the queries raised 
by Members may be sent to the Secretariat within a week, by the respective Ministries and other 
stakeholders. The witnesses assured the same. 
(The witnesses then withdrew)

At the outset, the Chairman welcomed the Members of  the Committee and the witnesses/ 
experts/ stakeholders of various agencies linked to  the ‘Sagarmala Projects’ initiative to the 
meeting and apprised them of the agenda of the meet ing. He asked the witnesses to give their 
views/ suggestions on the subject Progress made in implementation of Sagarmala Projects’ to 
gain insights on intended targets for development, recognizing and eliminating the lacunae faced 
by them in the programme. Thereafter, the Chairman desired to be apprised of the key 
interventions required to be undertaken to mobilize  financial resources, increase productivity of 
Indian ports as per international maritime benchmar ks, build India as a trans-shipment hub of 
cargo handling, build effective end-to-end supply c hain logistics, enable port-driven 
industrialization and digitization, reduce logistic costs, upgrade maritime infrastructure, train and 
deploy efficient maritime staff to propel Indian to the forefront of the Global Maritime Sector. 
2. The representative of NTCPWC, IIT Madras expressed their desire to effectuate port-led 
industrialization to enhance the overall port econo my, develop seamless port-related operations 
like cargo movement, inter-linkages between the por ts, modernisation, digitize port-activities, 
develop deep drafted ports, target bulk cargo recei ving-capacity, develop transhipment hubs, 
invite investors and industries through port-relate d industrialisation, improve port-linkages and 
develop rail-road evacuation routes. He emphasized the need to make efforts to improve inland 
shipping and coastal shipping in terms of seamless cargo movement through waterways and the 
54

 
need to eliminate lacunae in dredging, lack of tech nology availability, replacing outmoded 
technology at ports with state-of the art technology etc. 
3. The Representative of Pushpak Logistics Solutions i nformed the Committee about the 
lacunae and measures needed thereof in the areas su ch as: rigid permission procedures of the 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways in the Bill  of Coastal Goods, need to scrap custom 
duty on internationally travelling vessels, need to  match vessel volumes with global standards, 
assessing ports either scarcely or abundantly equip ped with technology infrastructure, increasing 
rebate for Vessel and Coastal Related Charges, lowe ring percent GST levied on Multimodal 
transportation, bringing private ports under the pu rview of the ‘Coastal Berth Scheme,’ rail-road 
connectivity etc. He mentioned the benefit coastal shipping has bestowed on his company 
through freight cost reduction as his company has a lso been working on green logistics, 
connecting major ports to minor ports and implement ing European model of transportation in 
Inland waterways. He desired to congregate, if made  feasible, the reports from other agencies to 
target cargo development in Sagarmala. 
4. The Representative of Mumbai to Mandwa Ferries made a brief presentation. Meanwhile, 
the Representative of Maharashtra Maritime Board ma de suggestions viz.  need for backup land 
for acquisition development, rail-road connectivity  and dredging to make port-led 
industrialization a reality, need to have guidelines in the Indian Vessels Act regarding ditching of 
old vessels/ cargo, need for subsidy in buying new vessels etc. 
5. Thereafter, the Representative of Indian National Shipowners’ Association INSA, made a 
powerpoint presentation. The Representative of Indi go Seaways Pvt. Ltd. succinctly suggested 
the Committee to take steps to reduce excessive reg ulatory intervention by Director General, 
Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways in safety /clearance aspects and also to provide 
flexible rules to build India as a trans-shipment h ub and attract more vessels to ports. The 
55

 
Committee was apprised of the lacunae i.e. building  sustainable infrastructure with adequate 
draft, rules for trouble-free cargo/ cargo storage handling, time-savvy e-clearances doorway/ 
apparatus to port vessels in a time-bound manner wi th reduced human intervention, de-
congesting entrances to the roads connecting the ports and terminals, globally competitive freight 
costs, promoting freight transportation through inl and waterways, ease of doing business rules 
for incoming & outgoing vessels, provision to grant Sea-time Certificates to mariners/ workers in 
the shipping sector, leveraging new technologies in  supply-chain logistics, removing taxation 
support bottlenecks, providing comparative infrastr ucture to maritime activities, digitization of 
custom-clearance processes and need to have specifi ed clearance process for all ports and 
adopting international maritime benchmarks to impro ve cost-competitiveness and EXIM 
business etc.  
6. Thereafter, the Representative of JM Baxi Group of Companies raised concern over the 
stern nature of Model Concession Agreement framewor k document under the Maritime Vision 
2030 on the basis of which a project can be privati zed as it is non bankable, it leaves little scope 
for negotiation. He addressed several more issues n amely lack of advancement in designing 
future projects, lack of integrated port developmen t, easing blanket ban and custom rules for 
implementation of new Inland Container Depots (ICDs ), easing licensing-rules for innovative 
projects, creating a mixed urban-commercial develop ment route through Build-Operate-Transfer 
(BOT) projects, forcing speedy execution of projects stagnated at port-level etc.  
7. The Chairman then queried the stakeholders regardin g changes made in banking and 
asked their ideas/ suggestions to implement project s through best practices employed by global 
ports, port-handling and promoting cruise/foreign t ourism globally through tourist-ships 
equipped with world-class facilities. Thereafter, t he Members raised several issues and queries 
regarding immigration, carbon emission statistics, dredging, lack of full-fledged coastal cargos in 
56

 
inland waterways, corruption in Maritime Boards’ sh ip-transportation business, lack of 
local/public transportation in port-peripheries, se curity issues arising with PPP model 
implementation, wider promotion of shipping transpo rtation, culturally equipped maritime 
development, feasibility studies to widen/deepen th e navigational channel through determination 
of vessel/ cargo draft length, profits generated by  cruise ship stations, easy loan facility to port-
owners/operators, port-linkages, etc. One Member su ggested the Committee to discuss with the 
Secretary, Ministry of Ports, Shipping, & Waterways, the issues raised by the stakeholders in the 
meeting. Another Member queried about the statistic s of crude-oil-ship volumes and port-rounds 
from Arab-Mediterranean Countries to Indian ports.  
8. After hearing the views of the witnesses, the Chair man of the Committee observed that 
shipping clearance delays and lack of labour around  ports has resulted in chaos which is 
dangerous in the ongoing pandemic situation and tha t changes are required to decongest roads 
connected to the ports. The witnesses also responde d to some of the queries raised by the 
Chairman and Members of the Committee. The Chairman directed them to furnish written replies 
to queries/points/issues raised by him and the Memb ers of the Committee, which could not be 
replied during the meeting, to the Secretariat.
